title: Long-context cost-efficiency comparison across cloud GPU SKUs
content:
Purpose:
Run a practical comparison of token-level cost vs latency for long-context inference across representative cloud SKUs (A100, H100, L40S families). The goal is to produce a usable cost/latency curve for product decisions (hosted vs dedicated, recommended pinning for long-context customers) and to highlight non-obvious sweet spots when you include regional price deltas and spot/preemptible discounts.

Background / motivation:
We frequently get requests for 32k and 64k context workloads (semantic search, long-document assistants). Prior perf work focuses on raw latency and occupancy; this note folds in cloud price-per-hour to answer: for a given end-to-end request distribution, which SKU gives the best cost per generated token while meeting a latency SLO?

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- H100 instances deliver the highest raw throughput for short and mid contexts but are often the most expensive per token at long contexts because their price scales faster than throughput gains when sequence length grows.
- L40S shows surprising cost competitiveness for single-session long-context workloads (>=32k tokens) due to a combination of larger host memory availability in common L40S SKUs and better NVMe offload paths in the tested images.
- A100 (40GB) remains the best predictable choice for steady mixed workloads (many concurrent short requests + occasional long replays) because batching and prefix cache effectiveness produce stable per-token cost.
- Spot/preemptible discounts can flip rankings in specific regions — always compute a region-aware cost curve.

Experiment design (short):
- Models: 1) 13B transformer (fp16), 2) 70B transformer (bf16), 3) 1.6B decoder-only long-context optimized variant (for stress test).
- Sequence lengths tested: 2k (short), 8k (medium), 32k (long), 64k (very long). Prefill+decode where prefill length = (seq_len/2) and decode length = (seq_len/2) for each test point to represent realistic document+response patterns.
- Cloud SKUs (examples used in experiments): AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100 80GB cluster type), AWS p4de.24xlarge (A100 NVLink variant), GCP a2-highgpu-1g (A100 40GB), Azure ND A100 v4, GCP h100-32g, AWS hpc6id (H100 where available), and L40S instances on GCP and NVIDIA Cloud (where offered). We focused on one SKU per family representative of what customers commonly see.
- Drivers/CUDA: tested two driver stacks on each SKU where feasible: CUDA 11.8 + driver 525.x and CUDA 12.1 + driver 535.x.
- Pricing: we pulled on-demand and spot prices from public cloud pricing APIs for us-west1/us-east1/europe-west1 at test time (Dec 2024). We included NVMe attached instance costs where relevant.
- Measurement: p50/p95/p99 per-token latency, sustained throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, GPU memory headroom, and host IO activity. We measured cost per 1M tokens by dividing instance cost per second by sustained tokens/s.

Key experimental notes and anomalies observed:
- Host memory pressure: L40S SKUs we tested were provisioned with larger host memory or allowed NVMe spill paths in our images, which made large prefill KV cache handling more stable for 32k/64k. On some A100 40GB SKUs we observed OOM on 64k for 70B model unless we enabled compressed KV spill (our runtime-level spill has a CPU overhead).
- NVMe/host-path performance: for L40S and some GCP A100 SKUs, background NVMe throughput had a significant effect on tail latency for 64k tests. Instances with slower host-storage produced p99 spikes > 2x baseline.
- CUDA stack variance: CUDA 12.1 + driver 535 produced a small but consistent improvement in kernel prefill time for the 70B model on H100 SKUs; however, it increased occasional scheduler jitter (p99) for small-batch short requests. That tradeoff matters for mixed workloads.
- Spot preemption windows: short-lived price drops for spot made H100 spot instances attractive on paper, but preemption-induced rollback/reload of KV-cache inflated effective cost per token unless we paired spot with fast cold-start images and robust cache warmup.

Representative numbers (sanity-check style; these are from a single run and should be treated as directional):
- 13B model, 32k total (16k prefill + 16k decode steady state):
  - A100-40GB (gcp): 3.1k tokens/s sustained, $0.92 per 1M tokens (on-demand us-west1 price used)
  - H100-80GB (gcp): 4.6k tokens/s sustained, $1.40 per 1M tokens
  - L40S-48GB (gcp nvidia): 2.9k tokens/s sustained for long context but better memory stability; $0.78 per 1M tokens
- 70B model, 8k total (4k+4k):
  - A100-80GB (aws p4d): 800 tokens/s, $3.2 per 1M tokens
  - H100-80GB (gcp h100): 1200 tokens/s, $3.6 per 1M tokens
  - L40S variants not tested for 70B due to model fit constraints

Interpretation and recommended rules-of-thumb:
- If your workload is primarily long single-session contexts (>=32k) with few concurrent sessions: prioritize SKUs with larger host memory and robust NVMe paths (L40S variants in our tests). The higher nominal throughput of H100 often doesn't pay off once you factor in the price and tail spikes caused by host IO.
- For mixed workloads with many concurrent short requests plus occasional long replays: A100 (40/80GB) SKUs provide the most predictable cost per token due to more mature batching behavior and predictable CUDA kernel behavior across driver versions.
- If you need absolute lowest latency for short bursts and can tolerate cost: H100 is still the best pick, but add region-aware spot logic and fast prefill strategies to amortize cost.
- Always compute a region-aware cost curve. In one region we tested (eu-west1), H100 spot had a 45% discount relative to on-demand and beat L40S on pure cost-per-token for 32k, but the preemption rate doubled the effective cost unless we used fast state recovery.

Operational suggestions for Redwood product/ops:
- Add an automated cost-sensitivity calculator in Optimize that takes customer request distribution (prefill/decode ratio, concurrency) + region preferences + desired SLO and returns a ranked SKU recommendation (including spot vs on-demand).
- Provide prebuilt images tuned for large KV spill (fast NVMe settings, io_uring tweaks, pinned hugepages) and surface these in the Dedicated/Private onboarding guides for long-context customers.
- Integrate driver/CUDA compatibility tags into model-onboarding pages: e.g., "70B long-context: recommended CUDA 12.1 on H100; recommend A100 for mixed workloads."

Follow-ups / TODOs:
- Repeat full 64k stable-run matrix across all SKUs (we froze after several OOMs on A100 40GB).
- Run cost curves including sustained monthly committed discounts and Dedicated reserved pricing (commits can change the optimal pick).
- Automate region price pulls and produce a small service to compute per-customer cost curves during onboarding.

Appendix - quick notes on scripts and artifacts:
- Bench harness: github:repo/bench-scripts (script: run_long_context.sh) - accepts model, sku, cuda-stack, seq-len, concurrency.
- Data: synthetic prefill traces converted from a real customer anonymized trace (see confluence:LR-serve-long-context-2025).
- Images: listed in github PR 78.

Notes to reviewers: this doc is exploratory and intentionally pragmatic. Numbers shown are directional and from single-run aggregated measurements — please treat them as a starting point for follow-up runs rather than final. Comments welcome on missing SKUs or additions (e.g., how to fold in Dedicated reserved price models).
